h1: Shortening brew day to four hours without cutting corners
title: A Four Hour Brew Day Without Shortcuts | Craft Beer School
desc: How to shorten an all-grain homebrew day to about four hours by preparing ahead, heating faster and cleaning as you go, without hurting the beer.
teaser: Most brew days are long because of waiting, not brewing. Here is how to get an all-grain day down to four hours.
standfirst: An all-grain homebrew day often stretches to six hours or more. Most of that time is waiting for water to heat and cleaning at the end. Plan those away and four hours is realistic without touching the steps that make good beer.
sections:
Time a typical brew in a bag day and the pattern is clear. Heating strike water: 45 minutes. Mash: 60. Heating to the boil: 30 to 40. Boil: 60. Chilling: 30 or more in summer. Cleaning: 45. Plus weighing grain, hunting for the hydrometer and fixing a leaking tap.

The mash and the boil are where the beer is made. The rest is logistics. Logistics is what you cut.
Do the prep the night before

The biggest saving costs nothing. The evening before:

  • Weigh and crush the grain, or open the crushed bag and check it.
  • Weigh hops into labelled cups for each addition.
  • Fill the kettle with treated water, with the Campden tablet already in.
  • Clean and lay out every piece of kit, including the fermenter.
  • Write the timeline and the numbers you expect on a brew sheet.

That removes 30 to 45 minutes from the day and most of the stress. Many brewers who swear brew days take six hours have never timed how long they spend looking for things.

Heating 30 litres from tap temperature is slow on a home stove. A few ways to speed it up:

  • Start the heat as soon as you wake up, before breakfast.
  • Keep a lid on the kettle while heating strike water and while bringing wort up to the boil.
  • Insulate the kettle with a camping mat or a wrap, which helps heating and holds mash temperature.
  • Use two heat sources together if you have them, such as gas plus induction, or heat part of the water in a second pot.

In a warm Indian kitchen, your tap water starts closer to strike temperature than in colder countries, which is one advantage of brewing here.
The mash and boil: what you can trim and what you cannot

With modern, well-modified malt, conversion is usually complete well inside 60 minutes, often by 30 to 45. An iodine test on a few drops of mash liquid, which stays brown rather than turning blue-black once starch is gone, tells you when. Some brewers mash for 45 minutes and lose nothing. The body of the beer comes from mash temperature more than length, so watch the thermometer, not just the clock.

The boil is less flexible. Sixty minutes drives off dimethyl sulphide (DMS), the cooked sweetcorn flavour, sterilises the wort and extracts bitterness. Pilsner malt has more DMS precursor, so it wants a vigorous boil and often 90 minutes. Do not shorten the boil to save time. Our guide to brewing a lager at home explains why pale lagers are less forgiving.

Chilling is slow when tap water is warm. Pre-chill: run the chiller with tap water to bring the wort down to about 35 °C, then switch to a coil sitting in a bucket of ice water or finish in an ice bath. A sealed bucket of ice made the day before is cheap and saves a lot of time.

Clean during the waits. The mash is 60 minutes of nothing; wash the milling and weighing kit. The boil is another 60; clean the mash bag and the counter. When the wort goes into the fermenter, only the kettle and chiller are left. Our guide to a cleaning routine for after brew day covers the order that works.

For a 20 litre brew in a bag batch with prep done the night before and water heating at wake-up:

  • 0:00 strike water reaches temperature. Mash in.
  • 0:05 to 1:05 mash. Clean prep kit. Check temperature twice.
  • 1:05 lift and drain the bag. Heat to boil with lid on.
  • 1:35 to 2:35 boil, hops on schedule. Clean bag and mash kit.
  • 2:35 to 3:05 chill, whirlpool, settle.
  • 3:05 to 3:20 transfer, aerate, pitch, take gravity.
  • 3:20 to 4:00 clean kettle and chiller.

Notice nothing was cut from the mash or the boil.

A brew sheet with times, temperatures and volumes printed in advance turns a brew day into a checklist. It also tells you, on the next brew, which step overran. Keep the sheet with the beer's tasting notes and you will start to see which shortcuts showed up in the glass. Our guide to the first all-grain brew day has the steps to build your sheet from.

Your first step: on your next brew day, write the clock time at the start of each step, then look at where the gaps were.
faqs: Can I shorten the mash to 45 minutes?
Often yes, with well-modified malt. An iodine test shows when starch conversion is complete.
Can I shorten the boil to save time?
It is better not to. A 60 minute boil drives off DMS and sterilises the wort. Pilsner malt usually wants 90 minutes.
What saves the most time on brew day?
Preparing the night before: weighing grain and hops, filling the kettle and laying out clean kit.
How do I chill wort faster in a hot climate?
Pre-chill with tap water to about 35 °C, then finish with a coil in ice water or an ice bath.
